summary: This note covers the California Gold Rush, which ran roughly from 1848 to 1855 after gold was found at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California. It describes the flood of about 300,000 people into California, the economic boost and fast-track statehood through the Compromise of 1850, and the severe population decline among Native Californians. It also notes how San Francisco publisher Samuel Brannan spread the news. The text is partly duplicated in the source.
one_line: Overview of the 1848-1855 California Gold Rush, its population boom, statehood, and devastating effects on Native Californians.
key_facts: The California Gold Rush lasted from 1848 to 1855.
Gold was found by James W. Marshall at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, on January 24, 1848.
The news of gold brought approximately 300,000 people to California from the rest of the United States and abroad.
The sudden influx of immigration and gold into the money supply reinvigorated the American economy.
California became one of the few American states to go directly to statehood without first being a territory, in the Compromise of 1850.
The Gold Rush had severe effects on Native Californians, causing a precipitous population decline from disease, genocide and starvation.
By the time the Gold Rush ended, California had gone from a thinly populated ex-Mexican territory to the home state of the first presidential nominee for the new Republican Party, in 1856.
Rumors of the gold discovery were confirmed in March 1848 by San Francisco newspaper publisher and merchant Samuel Brannan.
Samuel Brannan hurriedly set up a store to sell gold prospecting supplies.
Samuel Brannan walked through the streets of San Francisco holding aloft a vial of gold, shouting "Gold! Gold! Gold from the American River!"
The note contains a duplicated passage describing the start date, the 300,000 arrivals, and the statehood and population decline effects.
